tools.name: abilities
tools.description:
Lists every ability a creature has, not only those on its quickbar: its `talents`, `spells`, `skills`, and the abilities of its `items`. A skill with ranks has one entry per rank. `count` is the game's own total.

Each entry has the ability's id and name, and:
- `ready`: whether it can be used now. This is the same check the quickbar uses to gray out a button (mana or stamina, cooldown, anything stopping it). When false, `why` gives the reason, such as "Insufficient stamina". For a sustained ability that is switched on, the check includes its ongoing cost.
- `cost`: its mana or stamina cost, including fatigue.
- `cooldown`: while one runs, the seconds `remaining` of the `total`. This includes an item's ability, such as a poultice already drunk.
- for an item's ability: the `items` that give it (id, tag, name, stack) and how many are `held`. Use one with `order` action=ability and `item` or `itemTag`.

id.description: Who to read, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

tools.name: board
tools.description:
Reads and answers the quest board while its screen is open (the Chanter's board, or Awakening's Letters for the Commander). To open it, use the board placeable.

`action` is one of:
- look (default): returns the board's `entries`, each with `index`, `name`, `plot` (the quest's resource name), whether it is `accepted`, and its `text`.
- accept: accepts `entry`. Returns the entry and whether it is now `accepted`.
- close: closes the board, as its Close button does.

entry.description: For accept: the entry to accept, by its index, its name (any case) or its plot.

tools.name: camera
tools.description:
Reads or moves the camera, in explore or combat mode. `action`:

- `read` (the default): returns what it is `following`, its `focus` and how far that is from what it follows (`focusOffset`), its `position`, `facingDegrees` and `pitchDegrees`, whether it is `tactical`, `zoom` (1 close in, -1 the tactical view) and `zoomSetting`, the zoom it is easing toward. Its `projection` is what the last frame was drawn with, for drawing the same frame elsewhere: `fovDegrees` (vertical), `aspect` (width over height, as used), `near` and `far` in metres, the view's `width` and `height` in pixels, and Direct3D's row-major `matrix`. While another plugin's free view flies (flycam mode), `read` gives only the projection.
- `face`: turns it at once so that `target` or `point` is straight ahead, beyond the focus, for a screenshot that shows it. With `tilt` true it tilts as well, so the target is in the middle of the picture: use it for something above or below, such as the sky. A creature's point is at its feet, so one standing near is looked down on.
- `follow`: makes it follow `target` and jump there at once, as selecting a party member does (nothing gets selected). Use it to look at a creature elsewhere, or to centre the tactical view on one.
- `turn`: turns it to `facingDegrees`, tilts it to `pitchDegrees`, or both. The tactical view keeps its own pitch of -45 degrees, so tilt close in.
- `behind`: turns it to look the way `target` faces, from behind it, as the game's own camera reset does. Default: what it follows.
- `zoom`: sets `zoom` as the mouse wheel does: -1 is the tactical view, high above, and 0.5 (farthest) to 1 (closest) the close view. The game has no view between them. The camera eases there within about a second. In the tactical view the game pans the camera while the mouse is at the picture's edge or off it, so the party drifts to a corner (`focusOffset` grows): first hold the cursor inside the picture with `pointer` (a `pixel` near the middle), then `follow` a creature to centre on it.

Every action returns the camera as `read` does. A turn or tilt shows from the next frame, so take the screenshot after this call; after `zoom`, read until `zoom` has arrived. A mod that smooths camera moves treats a move from here as the player's and stops its own.

target.description: With `face`, `follow` or `behind`: the creature or object, by id.

point.description: With `face`: a world point, {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

tilt.description: With `face`: also tilt, so the target is in the middle of the picture and not only ahead. Default false: the tilt stays as it is.

facingDegrees.description: With `turn`: the way the camera looks, measured as a creature's `facingDegrees`, so a creature's turns the camera the way it looks: 0 along -y, -90 along +x, 90 along -x, 180 along +y.

pitchDegrees.description: With `turn`: -90 to 90. 0 is level, up positive, -90 straight down. Close in, the game keeps it between -60 and 60.

zoom.description: With `zoom`: -1 for the tactical view, or 0.5 (farthest) to 1 (closest) for the close view.

tools.name: character
tools.description:
Reads a creature's character sheet. It returns:
- race, gender, class, level, experience, rank, and `canLevelUp` with the `pointsToSpend`.
- the six `attributes`, each with total and base.
- `combat` numbers: attack, defense, armor, armor penetration, spellpower, weapon damage, fatigue and more.
- `health` and `manaStamina`, weapon style, and whether it is `plot` or `immortal`.
- for a party member, `follower`: its state, approval, whether it is locked in the party, and whether its own AI is on.
- `properties`: every property that is not zero, by the game's own names (resistances, regeneration, damage bonuses and so on).
- `equipment`: what it wears, slot by slot, in brief.

For more, call `equipment` (worn items in full), `inventory` (the backpack) or `creature` (effects and abilities).

id.description: Who to read, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

tools.name: chargen
tools.description:
Builds the hero on the game's character creation screen, as a player's clicks do, so the game's own rules and scripts apply; then ends the screen, and the origin starts. The screen must be up (`gui` shows CharGen, mode chargen): `game_new` starts a new game and brings it up. Pass `race`, `class` and `background` (and optionally `gender`, `voice`, `name`, `difficulty`), and either both `attributes` and `abilities` spending every point, or neither, and the game spends them as the screen's Quick Play does. A background must suit the race and class, as the screen allows: `offers`: true lists which. Choices are checked before anything is sent.

With `finish`: false the choices are made and the screen stays up; `offers` then also lists the skills and the talents or spells to choose from, and a later call (with every choice again) finishes. The answer has the `hero`, what it `chose`, the `exit` (full or quick play), the hero `after` (attributes, points left, ability count), the `origin` (its row of the origins table and its `startArea`), whether it `finished`, every message `sent`, and a `cursor`. The origin's opening follows: a cutscene, then a conversation.

race.description: human, elf or dwarf (or the race's id).

class.description: warrior, mage or rogue (or the class's id).

background.description: The origin's background by name, as `offers` lists them (noble, magi, dalish, city, commoner in the game as shipped), or its id.

voice.description: The sound set: a name from the game's player sound sets (ss_pc_mhuman_wise), or its last word for the hero's race and gender (wise, cocky, exp, mystic, sultry, suave, smart, violent; not every one for every race). Default wise, the screen's own.

name.description: The hero's name. Default the origin's own (Aedan for a human noble man), as the screen offers it.

attributes.description: Points by attribute, every one spent, as {"magic": 5}.

abilities.description: Ability ids to take, every point spent: the skills and the talents or spells `offers` lists as learnable, the first of a chain before the next.

difficulty.description: casual, normal, hard or nightmare, as the screen asks at its end. It is the game's option, kept in its profile's settings. Default: left as it is.

finish.description: End the screen once the hero is built, and so start the origin. Default true.

offers.description: List the backgrounds with the races and classes each takes, and, once a class is chosen, the hero's points and abilities to choose from. Sends nothing but the screen's own ability lookups.

tools.name: control
tools.description: Gives control to a party member, like clicking its portrait. Returns who was controlled `before`, who is `controlled` now, whether the change worked (`taken`), and a `cursor`. When the game keeps control where it was (at the party camp, in a conversation or a cutscene), `note` says so. `order` hands control over by itself when another party member has to move or use something.

id.description: The party member, by id; `state` lists the party.

tools.name: controls
tools.description: Lists the key bindings shown in the Options screen's Controls list: each action's `name`, `description`, and `primary` and `secondary` keys as displayed ("Ctrl + T", or "" for none). Actions added by plugins are included. Read only; works in any mode once the game has started.

match.description: Only actions whose name or description contains this text, in any case. Default: all.

tools.name: craft
tools.description:
Makes poisons, potions, traps and runes as the game's crafting screen does, so the game's own rules apply. `kind` picks the craft: poison, herbalism, traps or runes (Awakening's). The maker is `id`, a party member (default: the creature you control); no screen is opened and control stays where it is.

- Without `recipe`, lists the party's known recipes of the craft, as the screen shows them to the maker, and makes nothing. Each has its `id`, `name`, `product`, whether it `canMake` now, the `skill` rank it needs and whether the maker has it (`skillHeld`), and its `ingredients` with how many it needs and how many the pack has.
- With `recipe` (an id or a name from that list), makes it `count` times, one at a time, like the screen's Create button, for as long as the game allows.

The answer includes `made`, the recipe's `ingredients` afterwards, `done`, and `reason`: what ran short or which skill rank was missing, if it stopped. Recipes are bought from merchants.

kind.description: The craft whose recipes to use.

id.description: The maker, a party member's creature id. Default: the creature you control.

recipe.description: The recipe to make: its id (a number) or name, as the list shows. Omit it to list the recipes.

tools.name: creature
tools.description:
Returns one creature in full: the summary `creatures` gives (including the `command` it is carrying out), plus:

- `facingDegrees`, the way it looks: 0 along -y, -90 along +x, 90 along -x, 180 along +y, as `camera` and `stage_spawn` take it. And `appearance`.
- `abilities`: those on its quickbar and in its tactics, each with its cooldown (seconds left, out of how many).
- `path`: its current movement path; `beingWalked` says whether it is walking it now.
- `effects`: every effect on it, with its type (an EFFECT_TYPE_* name), creator, ability (id and name) and time left in seconds (null for effects that do not expire).

id.description: The creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

tools.name: creatures
tools.description:
Lists every creature in the area, nearest first. Each has its `id`, `name`, `tag`, `template`, `position`, `distance`, whether it is `dead`, its `health` and `manaStamina`, `combatState`, `attackTarget`, the `command` it is carrying out, and:

- `side`: party, hostile or neutral, as seen by the creature you control (or the hero if none).
- `group`: the game's own faction number: 0 the player's, 1 hostile, 2 friendly.
- `room`: the room it stands in (`number`), whether the party has `seen` it (never, in view or before; a room never seen is drawn black, along with everything in it), whether it is `shown`, how much the game wants it (`wanted`: dropped, kept, now) and whether it is in memory (`load`). Null where the area has no rooms.

`creature` gives one creature in full detail.

near.description: Measure distances from this creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Only those within this many meters of `near`. Default: the whole area.

side.description: Only creatures on this side. Default: all sides.

includeInactive.description: Also list creatures the area keeps hidden. Default false; then `inactiveLeftOut` says how many were left out.

brief.description: Return one line per creature (`lines`: id, name, tag, side, health, dead, distance) instead of full detail. Default false.

tools.name: cursor
tools.description:
Returns what is under the real mouse cursor right now, in explore and combat mode: `object`, what a click would act on (null if nothing), the `ground` point under it and whether it is `walkable`, and `hits`, everything the cursor's ray meets, nearest first (up to 8).

After moving the real mouse, check here before clicking: a click just beside a creature is a move order. The game updates this 15 times a second. Empty `hits`, not even ground, means the cursor is over the interface (including a creature's name label) or outside the game's picture.

tools.name: data
tools.description:
Reads the game's data tree, the values its interface displays. Use it to read what a screen shows without a screenshot.

Pass a dotted `path` ("GUI.SelectedChar", "Map.ShowAllLabels", "GUIPopupLayer.DialogBoxText") to get its value as `text` and as `number`, and its `type`; or pass `paths` to read several at once (`values`). `found` is false for a path that does not exist.

With `members: true`, it lists the members of the list at `path` (e.g. Container.Inventory, or the level-up screen's chains): their `count` and each member's path, which you can read the same way. Read only; works in any mode once the game has started.

path.description: A dotted path in the data tree.

paths.description: Up to 64 paths to read together.

members.description: List the members of the list at `path` instead of reading its value. Default false.

tools.name: dialogue
tools.description:
Reads or answers the conversation on screen, or skips a cutscene. While a conversation is open, `health` reports mode `dialog`.

`action`:
- `look`: returns the conversation: the `line` spoken last, its speaker, `by` and `to`, the conversation's `owner`, and the `replies` you can choose from now, each with its `place`. `cutscene` and `movie` say whether one is playing.
- `choose`: picks the reply at `place` (as `look` lists them), like clicking it.
- `continue`: like the skip key. It cuts the current line short and shows its replies, and goes through a reply with no text.
- `skip_cutscene`: like Escape in a cutscene or a pre-rendered movie.

With `until: "choice"`, the call carries on to the next real choice. A choice the game ignored is made again, replies with no text are gone through, and lines play at normal speed (`skipLines: true` cuts each short). The answer lists every line spoken on the way (`lines`: the speaker as the file names it, `by` and `to` as creatures, and the text), then either the `replies` of the next choice, or `ended` and the `mode` after (explore, a cutscene, a fight, an area loading).

Without `until`, the answer says the game was asked and gives a `cursor`: call `wait_for` from it on eluvian.dialogue.chosen, eluvian.dialogue.line or eluvian.mode.changed.

action.description: What to do; each action is described above.

place.description: With `choose`: which reply, counting from 0, as `look` lists them.

until.description: "choice" carries on to the next real choice or the end of the conversation. Default "step": one step only.

skipLines.description: With `until`: cut each line short. Default false.

budgetMs.description: The longest an `until` call may take, in milliseconds. Default 60000.

tools.name: equip
tools.description:
Puts an item from the pack on a party member, or takes one off, the way the inventory screen does, so the game's rules apply (requirements, which items fit which slot).

`action` is one of:
- equip (default): puts `item` in `slot`. Whatever the slot held goes back to the pack. Returns what the slot held `before` and holds `after`, and whether it worked (`equipped`). If it did not, the answer says whether the game thinks the creature can use the item (`canUse`), with its `requirements` and `restrictions` where known.
- unequip: takes `item` off and puts it in the pack. Returns whether it came off (`unequipped`).

It acts on `id`, by default the party member selected in the interface, and selects nobody: the selection and control stay as they were.

item.description: The item, by its id from `inventory` or `equipment`.

slot.description: For equip: the slot, by name (main, offhand, ring1, ring2, ...) or number. Default: the first slot the item fits.

id.description: The party member, by creature id. Default: the one selected in the interface.

tools.name: equipment
tools.description:
Lists what a creature wears, with each item in full, as `item` returns it: name, tag, template, base type, material, value, stats (armor, damage, defense, attack, crit chance, armor penetration, fatigue, optimum range and more, by the game's own names), properties with their power, and what using it does.

`slots` holds main, offhand and ammo for the weapon set in hand, then chest, head, boots, gloves, cloak, ring1, ring2, neck and belt. `weaponSet` is the set in hand, and `otherWeapons` is the other set.

id.description: Who to read, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

tools.name: events
tools.description:
Returns the events since a cursor, in order: what happened in the game (topics `eluvian.*`) and what mods emit (under their own prefix). Each event has its sequence number, frame and time.

The answer includes `next`, the cursor to pass as `since` next time (other tools' answers call theirs `cursor`), and `missed`, how many events were too old to keep.

Without `since` it reads from the oldest event held, not from now. To see what an action causes, call with `since: "end"` first, act, then read from the `next` it returned. Filter with `topic` and `match`; `describe` lists the topics instead.

topic.description: A topic ("eluvian.command.ended"), a prefix ("mymod.*"), "*", or an array of these. Default: every topic.

match.description: Payload fields the event must have, with equal values; nested objects match as subsets. Creatures are ids like "0x7d9": {"id": "0x7d9"}.

since.description: Where to start reading: `next` from the last read, or `cursor` from another tool's answer. "end" returns no events and `next` set to now, to read from after acting. Default 0: the oldest event still held.

limit.description: The most events to return. Default 100.

describe.description: If true, lists the topics (those matching `topic`), what each means and what its payload holds, instead of reading events. Default false.

tools.name: exits
tools.description:
Lists the ways out of the area: every door, other placeable or trigger that takes the party to another area, nearest first. Each has `leadsTo` (the destination area's tag and waypoint), its `kind` (placeable or trigger), `position`, `distance` and whether it is `active`.

The easiest way to leave is `travel` with `exit` (an id from here) or `area`. By hand, use a placeable with `order` action=use, and walk into a trigger by moving to its position. Some doors only decide where they lead when used, so their `leadsTo` may be empty or show the last destination. Leaving loads the other area, and the game may autosave.

near.description: Measure distances from this creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Only those within this many meters of `near`. Default: the whole area.

brief.description: Return one line per exit (`lines`) instead of full detail. Default false.

tools.name: frame_capture
tools.description: Records the next frame the game draws, as Direct3D 9 was handed it: each draw call with its vertex and pixel shaders (by `id`, a hash of the bytecode, the same in every run), their constants by name with the values the device held (of each register as many floats or ints as the constant's type uses, a float1 one, a float4x4 sixteen; a bool each), the textures each sampler had (the .dds file), the primitive counts and the render states asked. What the engine was drawing: `material` (its .mao, no extension) for a draw a material makes, and for a mesh's or cloth's also `model`, `mesh` (the node's name in the model) and `object` and `node`, addresses that group one object's draws in the frame; none for the interface, full-screen passes and most effects. `shaders` lists each listed draw's shaders once, with their constant tables. A frame has some 2,000 draws, so the answer lists `most` (20) of those matching `texture` (part of a .dds name), `shader` (the start of an id), `material` and `model` (part of the name), after `skip`; `constants` keeps only the values named. `file` writes every draw of the frame, unfiltered, for a diff with another engine's. The game must be drawing: a fullscreen game minimised draws nothing. Recording slows that one frame a little.

states.description: Render states to read at each draw, by name (ZENABLE, ALPHABLENDENABLE, or D3DRS_ZENABLE) or number. Default: depth, blending, alpha test, cull mode, colour writes, sRGB writes and stencil.

texture.description: List only draws sampling a .dds whose name has this.

shader.description: List only draws whose vertex or pixel shader id begins with this.

material.description: List only draws whose material's name has this.

model.description: List only draws whose model's name has this.

constants.description: List only these constants' values, by name. Default: all.

skip.description: Matching draws to pass over first. Default 0.

most.description: Matching draws to list at most, 0 to 100000. Default 20.

file.description: A path to write the whole frame to as JSON, every draw and its values.

timeout.description: Milliseconds to wait for the frame, 100 to 30000. Default 5000.

tools.name: geometry
tools.description:
Measures from a creature (`id`) to another creature or object (`target`) or a `point`. Returns the straight-line distance, the line of sight as the engine judges it (eye height to eye height, and where it is blocked, if it is; only walls and placeables block it, not creatures), and the creature's current movement path with its length and how much is left. `beingWalked` says whether it is walking that path now.

With `walk: true`, it also asks the game's pathfinder for the path the creature would walk there now: `found` and its `length`, or why not. If a shut door or similar is in the way, `blocker` names it: use it first, then move. The creature is not moved.

id.description: The creature to measure from, by id. Default: the creature you control.

target.description: The creature or object to measure to, by id.

point.description: The point to measure to: {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

walk.description: Also find the path the creature would walk there: its length, or what is in the way. Default false.

trace.description: With `walk`: include the path search's internal log, for diagnosing a search that failed. Default false.

waypoints.description: List the points along the paths. Default false.

tools.name: gift
tools.description:
Gives a follower a gift from the pack, like the inventory's Give button. It raises the game's own gift event, so the game's scripts change the approval and move the item, and a special gift may start a conversation.

Pass `to`, a follower in the party, and `item`, an item of base type Gift from `inventory`. The call returns once the game has taken the gift (the item left the pack or the approval changed), or after `budgetMs`. The answer includes the approval before and after (`approvalBefore`, `approvalAfter`), whether the item left the pack (`given`), the game's `mode` afterwards (`dialog` means a conversation began: answer it with `dialogue`), and a `cursor` for the events that followed.

budgetMs.description: The longest to wait for the game to take the gift, in milliseconds. Default 3000.

tools.name: gui
tools.description:
Returns what the game's interface is showing. Call it when `health` reports mode gui, or when the game seems to be waiting on something. Works in any mode. The answer includes:

- `screens`: the screens shown now, top first, each with its `name` (Inventory, Store, WorldMap, PartyPicker, CharacterRecord, Map, Journal, Skills, Options; Main is the HUD), `movie` and `layer`.
- `fullScreen`: the name of the full-screen screen that is open (inventory, map, journal...), or null.
- `fullScreenHidden`: present when a full-screen screen is still open in the game but not drawn, e.g. after WorldMap.WorldMapClosed alone. Clear it with `input` {"message": "GUI.HideFullScreenGUI"}, as a Close button does.
- `popup`: the game's message box, with its text and each button's label and what pressing it sends. A message box blocks the game until answered, and nothing else reports it, so check here when a load or an order was accepted but nothing happened.
- `loot`: the loot panel a container opens (a chest, remains, a pile of bones), part of the Inventory screen: its `container`, the `items` in it, the `backpack`'s item count and limit, and its `buttons`, Take All and Close, with what each does.
- `store`: with a merchant's Store screen open, the `stock` with each item's `price`, your `pack` with what each item `sellsFor`, the `money` (in copper) and the markups.

To act on these: `press` presses a message box or loot panel button; `loot` walks to a container, opens it and takes everything in one call; `store` buys and sells.

tools.name: health
tools.description:
Says whether the game is alive and what state it is in. Call it first. It answers without waiting for a game frame, so it works while an area loads or the game hangs.

`state` is one of:
- running: frames are coming.
- stalled: no frame for over a second (an area loading, a modal dialog, or a hang).
- starting: no frame yet.

The answer also includes the game `mode`, whether it is `paused`, the calls waiting for a frame (`callsWaiting`), the event `cursor` to pass as `since` to `wait_for`, which plugins have registered tools, who started the game (`owner`) and, where several copies of the game run, which one this is (`instance`, null for the game as ever).

tools.name: input
tools.description:
Sends the game one of its own internal messages, written as text. Use it when no other tool fits, as `script` is for script commands. The game does whatever the message means, so know what it does before sending it. Pass exactly one of:

- `message`: what an interface button sends, as "Receiver.Message arguments" (for example "GUIPopupLayer.ScriptDialogResult 1 1 -1"; `gui` shows what each button of a message box sends).
- `binding`: what a key's binding names, as "Message arguments", sent the way a key press sends it (for example "UserTogglePauseMessage" or "SelectPartyMemberIndexMessage 0 1").

A text that saves the game is refused unless `confirmSave` is true: the quicksave key's "SaveGameMessage -1 2" overwrites the player's quicksave. The answer's `sent` is false if the engine knows no such receiver or message; it also includes a `cursor`. `movie` reaches what no message does.

confirmSave.description: Send a text that saves the game anyway. Default false.

tools.name: inventory
tools.description:
Lists the items in a creature's backpack, or in a container without opening it (a chest, a body, a pile of bones). The hero's backpack is the party's. Worn items are not included; `equipment` lists those.

The answer has `count` and `items`, each in brief (name, tag, template, base type, stack, value, plot). For a creature it also has `holds` (the most the backpack can hold) and `money` (the party's).

A container's contents may only be decided when it is opened, so an empty list does not mean it is empty. The `loot` tool opens a container and takes what is inside.

id.description: The creature or container, by id (containers come from `placeables`). Default: the hero.

full.description: Return each item in full, as `item` does. Default false.

tools.name: item
tools.description: Reads one item in full: name, tag, template, base type, material, `stack` and `maxStack`, value, the slot it is worn in (`equippedIn`), its stats, its properties with their power, what using it does (`ability`), and whether it is plot, droppable or indestructible.

id.description: The item, by its id from `inventory` or `equipment`.

tools.name: journal
tools.description:
Lists the quests in the journal: `active`, the quest currently marked, and `quests`, those in progress. Each quest has its `plot` name (pass it to `plot` for its flags), its `name`, `description` and `objective` as the journal shows them, its `group` and `area`, whether it was `updated` or is `completed`, and `parent` if it is part of another quest. A finished quest may stay in `quests` with `completed` true.

Finished quests are only counted (`completedCount`) unless you pass `completed: true`. Read only.

completed.description: Also list the finished quests. Default false.

tools.name: levelup
tools.description:
Spends a creature's level-up points as the game's level-up screen does, by the engine's own rules for what may be taken. `id` picks the creature (default: the creature you control). The tool spends the points and completes the level-up; with `showMs` above 0 it shows the level-up screen meanwhile, where the screen can open. Pass exactly one of:

- `offers: true`: returns what the screen offers and spends nothing: `points`, `attributes`, and the class's `talents`, `spells` and `skills`, each a list of abilities with `id`, `name` and `state` (`has`, `learnable` now, or `not yet`); and the `specializations`, each with `id`, `name` and `state` (`has`, `learnable`, `locked` or `no point to spend`).
- The points to spend: `specialization`, `abilities` and `attributes`, in any combination. A specialization is taken first, so its abilities can be taken in the same call. List `abilities` with the first of a chain before the next. The first one refused (had already, locked, not offered, or no point left) stops the tool, saying why; those taken before it are kept (`taken`).
- `auto: true`: the screen's Auto Level Up, which spends every point as the game chooses for the class (all a follower needs), repeating while points are left.

The answer includes `levelled`, `reason`, `before` and `after` (level and points to spend), the `attributes` raised and by how much, the talents, spells and skills `gained`, and a `cursor`; `screen` says why the screen was not shown, where it was asked for and did not open. It refuses a creature with no points to spend (`character` shows `canLevelUp`). A level-up is permanent once the game is saved.

id.description: Who levels up, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

auto.description: If true, spend every point as the screen's Auto Level Up does.

offers.description: If true, return what the screen offers and spend nothing.

abilities.description: Ability ids to take, in order, from those `offers` lists as learnable.

attributes.description: Points to put in each attribute, e.g. {"strength": 2, "cunning": 1}.

specialization.description: A specialization to take, by name or ability id, as `offers` lists it.

showMs.description: How long to show the level-up screen before the points are spent and after, in milliseconds, so whoever watches sees it. Default 1000; 0 for no screen.

tools.name: log
tools.description: Reads a DAOLib log (in Documents\BioWare\Dragon Age\daolib\) from a cursor. Returns the lines written since `since`, and `next`, the cursor to read from next time. `restarted` is true when the file began again because the game restarted. Without `file`, lists the logs.

file.description: The log's name: "loader", "eluvian", a mod's, or any other in the folder. Omit to list the logs.

since.description: The byte cursor to read from: `next` from the last read. "end" reads nothing and returns the end as `next`, to read from after acting. Default: the start of the file.

grep.description: Keep only the lines this regular expression matches.

limit.description: The most lines to return. Default 300.

tools.name: loot
tools.description:
Takes everything a container holds (a chest, a body's remains, a pile of bones: an id from `placeables`) in one call. The looter walks to `target` (like `travel`, opening doors on the way), uses it to open the game's loot panel, and takes everything like the panel's Take All button, which closes the panel. Without `target`, it takes from the loot panel open now.

The looter is the creature you control, or `id`, another party member, who is given control for the looting and gives it back afterwards (`controlled` says who has it).

The answer includes `looted`, `reason`, the `container`, what was `taken` and what is `left` (each item in brief), whether the backpack was `full` (the rest then stays, and so does the panel), whether the panel `closed`, and the `walk`. It stops and says why when the container does not open: it is locked, a fight or conversation starts, a message box appears, or there is nothing to take (`empty`: an emptied body's remains open no loot panel at all).

With `radius` instead of `target`, it loots every placeable within that many meters whose use is a loot or an unlock (`action` in `placeables`), nearest first. The answer has one report each in `containers`, the `count` looted, and what else was there in `skipped`. It passes locked or empty containers, and stops (`stopped`) at a fight, a conversation, a question or a full pack.

Some containers choose their treasure only when opened, so one that read as empty may not be. Read the events from `cursor` (`events` or `wait_for`) to see what followed: opening a container may start a fight or a plot step.

target.description: The container, by id. Default: the loot panel open now.

id.description: The party member who loots, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Loot every container within this many meters, instead of one `target`.

budgetMs.description: The longest the whole call may take, in milliseconds. Default 60000, or 300000 with `radius`.

showMs.description: How long to linger on the panel before Take All, in milliseconds, so whoever watches sees it. Default 1000; 0 for none.

tools.name: movie
tools.description:
Drives the ActionScript of a screen that is shown, to reach what no message does (such as a tab or a scroll). Pass `screen` (its name from `gui`, such as "Options") and exactly one of:

- `call`: call a function by its path, with `args`. For example "SceneManager.PlayScene" with ["Controls"] shows the Options screen's Controls page. Returns whether it `ran` and what it returned (`type` and `value`). "ExternalCommands.SendMessage" with one text sends what a button of the screen sends, and reaches what a plugin takes before the engine sees it: on the Options screen, ["ClientOptions.SetClientOptionMessage DAOLibMyOption 1"] ticks a checkbox a plugin added as MyOption (0 unticks; its clip is OptDAOLibMyOption_mc). `ran` then says only that the function ran, not that anything took the text.
- `get`: read a path. Returns its `type` and `value`.
- `set`: set a variable to `value`. Returns whether it was `done` and whether the path `existed`; setting a path that did not exist creates a new variable that nothing reads.
- `children`: list a clip's children, each with its `depth` and `path` (to `get` or `call` under).

An object or clip comes back as a string; a clip's string is its full path.

call.description: The path of an ActionScript function to call.

args.description: With `call`: the arguments, as strings, numbers or booleans. Default none.

set.description: The path of a variable to set.

value.description: With `set`: the new value, a string, number or boolean.

children.description: The path of a clip whose children to list.

placed.description: With `children`: also list clips built into the screen's design, not only those made while it runs. Default false.

tools.name: order
tools.description:
Gives an order to a creature by id, as the player would. `action`:

- `attack`: attack `target`.
- `move`: walk to `point`. Only the creature you control can be moved this way, so another party member `id` is given control first and keeps it (the answer says `controlled` and `before`). Creatures outside the party cannot be moved.
- `ability`: use `ability` (an id from `abilities`) on `target` or at `point`. For an item's ability, such as a potion's, also pass `item` or `itemTag`. An area ability with a range (such as Fireball; `abilities` gives each one's `aoe` and `range`) aimed at a creature is aimed at the ground under it (`aimedAt`), unless `atCreature` is true. An ability used on oneself alone (`targetType` 1 in `abilities`, such as a sustained mode) needs no `target`: by command it is aimed at the creature itself, which turns a mode on or off.
- `use`: use the object `target`, such as a door, chest or lever. Using a door toggles it; `doorWas` says whether it was open.

How the order is sent (`via`):
- `command`: through the engine's own order functions. The order counts as the player's, and anything watching the command queue sees it. Any creature can obey. A use by command does `objectAction`.
- `click`: as if the player clicked, so anything hooked to clicks also runs (for example a mod that asks for an ability's target when none is given). Only the creature you control can click, only in explore or combat mode, and a move cannot be clicked. An attack or use by click is carried out by every party member selected in the party bar (`selected`), and the answer cannot say who obeyed: check the events from `cursor`.

`via` defaults to `command`, except: a use without `objectAction` by the creature you control goes by click, since a click picks the object's own action (a plain use by command can leave a chest or door shut). Out of combat, an item's ability by the creature you control also goes by click, since by command it does nothing there. Out of combat, when `id` is another party member, control is handed to it first for these, as for a move, and stays with it.

The answer says the order was `given` and includes a `cursor`; `wait_for` from it shows what happened (eluvian.command.started and eluvian.command.ended, and a mod's own events).

id.description: Who obeys, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

atCreature.description: With `ability`: aim an area ability at the creature itself, not the ground under it. Default false.

target.description: The creature or object to act on, by id.

point.description: With `move` or `ability`: the point, {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

item.description: For an item's ability: the item's id.

itemTag.description: For an item's ability: the item's tag, looked up in the creature's inventory (for example gen_im_qck_health_101, a lesser health poultice).

via.description: How the order is sent. Default command, but click for a use without `objectAction`, or an item's ability out of combat, by the creature you control.

objectAction.description: With `use` by command: what to do with the object, a PLACEABLE_ACTION_* name such as open, close, unlock, use, examine, disarm, dialog, open_inventory, trigger_trap, topple or area_transition. Default use. It must be an action the object accepts in its current state, or the command ends with COMMAND_FAILED: a locked chest takes unlock, then open_inventory.

tools.name: party
tools.description:
Works the party picker, the screen the game shows after a follower joins and at camp, as a player's clicks do. It refuses when the picker is not open (`health` reports mode `partypicker` when it is).

`action`:
- `look`: returns who is `chosen` (each slot's id, name and tag), and everyone the picker `offered`, each with its `state`: chosen, available, unavailable, suspended or lockedActive (kept in the party by the story).
- `choose`: picks the follower `name`, as a click on them does.
- `unchoose`: removes the chosen follower `name`, like clicking their portrait.
- `clear`: removes everyone except the hero and those the story keeps.
- `accept`: confirms the party as chosen, and returns the `party` once the picker has closed.

Up to four can be chosen: unchoose one before choosing a fifth. A choice the picker refuses is an error saying why. `choose`, `unchoose` and `clear` refuse when the picker's `status` is not `use`, meaning the picker is only for viewing. A picker you open yourself with the script command ShowPartyPickerGUI may be view-only: call SetPartyPickerGUIStatus with 2 through `script` before opening it, so it can change the party.

action.description: What to do; each action is described above.

name.description: With `choose` or `unchoose`: a follower's name as the picker shows it, their tag, or their id.

tools.name: pause
tools.description: Pauses or unpauses the game, like the space bar. Returns whether it is `paused` afterwards. Other tools keep working while the game is paused.

paused.description: true to pause, false to unpause.

tools.name: peek
tools.description: Reads a field of a live object, or of the game's own data, by a chain of offsets: from the start, every offset but the last is a pointer read and followed, and the value is read at the last, as `type`. Use it to check a reading of the exe against the running game: a field at +0x64 of the object a creature holds at +0x7B0 is `{"object": "0x7d9", "offsets": ["0x7B0", "0x64"], "type": "f32"}`. Each pointer on the way is named by its class (RTTI). A read that fails is answered with `readable: false` and where, never a crash. Nothing is written.

object.description: An object's id, "0x7d9", as creatures, placeables or party list them.

side.description: With `object`: the game's object (CGameObject, the scripts' side), or the client's (CCObject, what is drawn). Default game.

address.description: In place of `object`: an address in the running game, "0x00b2b290".

address_id.description: In place of `object`: an ID of the address library (DAOLib's tools/address_ids.py names them), its address in the running build.

offsets.description: The chain: numbers, or hex as text ("0x7B0", "-0x10"). None reads at the start itself.

type.description: What the value is: a float, an integer, a pointer (with its class), three or four floats, the engine's std::wstring, or raw bytes as hex. Default u32.

count.description: How many values one after another (bytes: how many bytes, default 16). Default 1.

tools.name: placeables
tools.description:
Lists the doors, chests, levers and other placeables in the area, nearest first. Each has its `id`, `name`, `tag`, `template`, `position` and `distance`, and:

- `state`, the placeable's own state number (it changes when a door or chest opens), and `stateName`: shut, locked, open or destroyed.
- `action` and `actionName`: what using it does now (loot, unlock, open, use, ...).
- `active`, `interactive` (whether it can be used) and `popup`, its tooltip text.
- `lock`: whether it needs a key (`keyRequired`), the key's tag (`keyTag`), whether the party has it (`keyHeld`), and the lock-picking level needed (`pickLevel`).
- `leadsTo`, for a way out of the area: the destination area's tag and waypoint.

Use one with `order` action=use.

near.description: Measure distances from this creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Only those within this many meters of `near`. Default: the whole area.

includeInactive.description: Also list placeables the area keeps hidden. Default false; then `inactiveLeftOut` says how many were left out.

interactive.description: true: only those that can be used; false: only those that cannot. Default: both.

brief.description: Return one line per placeable (`lines`) instead of full detail. Default false.

tools.name: plot
tools.description:
Returns the state of a quest or story: the flags of the plot named in `plot`. Plot names are the game's plot files (and a mod's own), e.g. "bed000pt_main" or "gen00pt_party"; `resources` with type plo and `journal` list them.

The answer includes the plot's `name` as the journal shows it, its `flags`, each with `flag` (number), `name`, whether it is `set`, and the `journal` text of a set flag that has one, and `set`, the names of all set flags. Pass `flag` to get just that one.

Flags numbered 256 and up are normally computed by the plot's script, which this tool does not run; their values are what the game returns without it. Read only.

flag.description: One flag to read, by number or name. Default: all flags.

tools.name: pointer
tools.description:
Makes the game act as if the mouse rested at a place, without clicking, to show what appears only under the cursor (a path preview, a cost caption, a highlight). Pass one of `target`, `point` or `pixel`, or `release: true` to stop.

The game picks up the new place within about a fifteenth of a second: wait a quarter second, then `cursor` says what is under it and `screenshot` shows the rest. The real mouse is not moved or read, and the window need not be in front; the drawn cursor and the game's menus and bars still follow the real mouse. While the hold lasts, a click acts on the held place, not under the real mouse. It ends after `seconds` or on release.

The answer includes the place `pointed` at (as `screen` gives places), how long it `holds`, and whether the game window is in the `foreground`.

target.description: A creature or object, by id; the cursor goes where `screen` would aim.

point.description: A world point: {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

pixel.description: A pixel: [x, y] in the game's pixels.

seconds.description: How long to hold, up to 3600 seconds; 0 holds until released. Default 60.

release.description: Stop holding and give the cursor back to the mouse.

tools.name: press
tools.description:
Presses a button, just as a click would. If a message box is up, the button is one of its own; otherwise it is one of the loot panel a container opens: Take All or Close. `gui` shows both.

A box that asks for text (its `input` in `gui`, such as a name) takes `text` to type into it before the button; an empty field is refused unless `allowEmpty` is true. For a message box, the answer includes the button `pressed`, the `box` text and any `text` sent. Take All returns what was `taken`, what is `left` and whether the backpack was `full`, and closes the panel unless it was full.

button.description: The button's label (such as "Take All") or its position, counting from 0.

text.description: For a box with a text field: what to type into it before the button.

allowEmpty.description: Send a box's text field empty. Default false (refused).

tools.name: resources
tools.description:
Searches the game's resources by name, across every archive in the game's folder. Use it to find the name to pass to another tool:

- `utc`: creature templates, for `stage_spawn`.
- `uti`: item templates, for `stage_equip`.
- `plo`: plots, for `plot`.
- `cut`: cutscenes, for `stage_cutscene`.

Returns the matching names, sorted, each without its extension and with the archive it is in, up to `most`, and the `count` of all matches. The core and campaign archives are in every game; an add-in's resources only load where that add-in runs. The first call in a game reads every archive's index from disk and can take a minute or more, so give it a long timeout; later calls are fast.

type.description: The file extension to list: utc, uti, plo or cut. Default: all types.

match.description: Words that must all appear in the name, in any case, e.g. "hurlock archer".

most.description: The most names to return. Default 100.

tools.name: rooms
tools.description: Lists every room of the area: its `number`, whether the party has `seen` it (never, in view, before), whether it is therefore `shown` (a room never seen is drawn black, along with everything in it), how much the game `wanted` it and its `load`, and `party` true on the rooms the party stands in (`partyRooms`). With `point`, also the room `at` that point, and `outsideBy` how far the point lies outside its bounds (0 inside). Outdoors the rooms are the terrain's cells, and never read as loaded. A creature's own room is in `creature` and `creatures`.

point.description: A world point, {x, y, z} or [x, y, z]: also answer the room it is in.

shownOnly.description: Only the rooms the party sees or has seen. Default false.

tools.name: saves
tools.description:
Lists, loads and makes the game's saves. `action`:

- `list`: the saves of `character` (or of every character), each with its area, name, time played and level, as the load screen shows them.
- `load`: loads the save picked by `character`, `kind` and `number`, from the main menu or in the world. Refused during a conversation.
- `force_load`: presses the game's Force Load after a load it answered with "requires the following content" (`gui` shows that message). The game loads without that content, and such a game is never saved.
- `save`: makes a new manual save in the next free slot, named `name`. This is what a test should do, since it overwrites nothing.

Saving into a slot `number` that already holds a save, or with `kind` quick (the player's quicksave), is refused unless `overwrite` is true. The game also refuses to save in combat or a cutscene.

A load or save only asks the game: the answer includes a `cursor`, and `wait_for` eluvian.game.loaded or eluvian.game.saved from it says when it is done. If no load event comes, the game may be showing a message box; `gui` reads it.

action.description: What to do; each action is described above.

character.description: A character's save folder, such as "Aedan". Default: the character being played (or, with `list`, every character).

kind.description: The kind of save. Default manual.

number.description: The slot's number. Default for `load`: 1; for `save`: the next free slot.

overwrite.description: With `save`: allow writing over the save in slot `number`, or over the quicksave. Default false.

tools.name: scenario
tools.description:
Runs a list of steps in one call and returns a transcript. Steps can call tools, wait for events, pause, and check answers, so a whole test step fits in one call: order an attack, wait for the turn to end, check the target's health.

A wait starts from the cursor taken just before the latest tool step, so it does not miss what that tool set off. The run stops at the first failed step unless `continueOnError` is true. It takes at most 100 steps and runs within `budgetMs`: waits and sleeps are cut to the time left, and the run stops with `timedOut` when it is gone. A tool step already running in the game is always waited for to its end, because what it does cannot be undone.

The answer includes `ok`, `timedOut`, `stepsRun`, `elapsedMs`, and `steps`, one entry per step run.

steps.description:
The steps, 1 to 100, each one of:
- {"tool": name, "args": {...}, "as": label}: call a tool.
- {"waitFor": {"topic": ..., "match": {...}}, "timeoutMs": n, "since": cursor, "as": label}: wait for an event, like `wait_for`.
- {"sleepMs": n}: pause, at most 60000 ms.
- {"expect": {"from": label, "pointer": "/given", "equals" | "notEquals" | "exists" | "atLeast" | "atMost": value}}: check the answer of an earlier step labeled with `as`.
- {"until": {"tool", "args", "pointer", an expectation, "intervalMs"}, "timeoutMs": n, "as": label}: call a tool until a condition holds, like `wait_until`.
A step's `timeoutMs` defaults to 30000.

continueOnError.description: If true, keep going past a failed step. Default false.

budgetMs.description: The longest the whole run may take, in milliseconds. Default and maximum 600000 (ten minutes).

tools.name: screen
tools.description:
Finds where things are on the game's screen, for driving the real mouse. Always returns the `view` size and the game `window`. Pass any of:

- `target`: returns `aim`, a pixel to click it at, well inside the object and with nothing in front (null if it is out of view or hidden; `camera` can bring it into view). `clear` is how many of the eight pixels 10 away also hit it; 8 means well inside. `position` is where its feet are.
- `point`: returns the pixel where that world point appears.
- `pixel`: returns `hits`, what lies under that pixel, nearest first. The first object is what a click there would act on.

Each place is given as `x`, `y` (the game's pixels from the top left), `fx`, `fy` (fractions of the picture) and `desktop` (the desktop pixel to send a real mouse to). `coveredBy` names another window covering the game there, if any: a click there would hit that window, so move it or the game first. After moving the mouse, `cursor` says what the game has under it.

target.description: A creature or object to find, by id.

point.description: A world point to find: {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

pixel.description: A pixel to look under: [x, y] in the game's pixels.

tools.name: screenshot
tools.description:
Takes a picture of the game as it is now, interface included. Other windows on top of the game do not get in the way. `source`:

- `window` (the default): Windows draws the game's window at once, even while the game is not drawing frames. If the display is asleep or the session locked, the picture is all black (`black`); use `game` then.
- `game`: the game takes its own screenshot, as its screenshot key does, a frame or more later. While another plugin's free view flies (a photo camera's), the game hides its interface and that plugin keeps its own panel out of this picture, so it is the frame alone.

Returns the picture as an image, with its `width`, `height` and `file` (in Screenshots\Eluvian; for `game`, the game's own file is `original`). Pass `image: false` to get only the file and save tokens. `width` or `height` scales the picture, the other side kept to the frame's aspect; both must be the frame's aspect, or with `crop` true the middle of the frame at theirs is taken. The game draws at its window's size, so a larger picture is no sharper: `frame` is the size it was drawn at. To draw the same frame elsewhere, `camera`'s `projection` is the one it was drawn with.

source.description: Who takes the picture. Default window.

image.description: Include the picture itself in the answer. Default true.

width.description: The picture's width in pixels, 16 to 8192. Default: the frame's.

height.description: The picture's height in pixels, 16 to 8192. Default: the frame's.

crop.description: With both `width` and `height` of another aspect than the frame's: take the middle of the frame at theirs. Default false: refused.

tools.name: script
tools.description:
Calls any of the game's 661 script commands by name and returns its result (`value`). Use it when no other tool fits, for example GetCreatureProperty, GetRemainingCooldown or SetCreatureProperty. `action`:

- `call` (the default): run `command` with `args`.
- `find`: list the commands whose name contains `command` (any case).
- `describe`: show one command's parameters, their types and defaults.

Pass arguments in order (`args`: [...]) or by parameter name (`args`: {"oCreature": "0x7d9"}); any left out take their defaults. Objects are ids, and null is OBJECT_INVALID. Commands that take or return a location, effect, event or command cannot be called by name.

command.description: The command's name as the game's scripts spell it, or with `find` part of one.

args.description: With `call`: the arguments, as an array in parameter order or an object by parameter name. Default none.

tools.name: snapshot
tools.description: Takes the game's state in one frame, as a JSON another engine can write too, to compare with snapshot_diff: the same save and inputs run here and elsewhere, or this game at two moments. It has the area, mode, paused, `gameTime` (the world clock a save keeps, in seconds; `worldTime` the same as day and ms), the frame and an events `cursor`; every creature of the area, inactive ones too, keyed `tag|template#k` (k counts that tag and template in the order they were made), with position, facingDegrees, health and stamina, dead, active, group, combatState, attackTarget (a key), the command's type number and effects (type, ability, remaining); the party and the one controlled, by key. Pass `plots` for their flags by name, `vars` for variables, and `file` to keep it on disk for snapshot_diff. To line two runs up, pause, act, let the same game time pass, pause again, then take it.

plots.description: Plots whose flags to include, by resource name (bed000pt_main).

vars.description: Variables to include, each with object, name and type: object is module (the default), area, hero, controlled, a creature's key or an id; type is int (the default), float, string or object. A variable the object's scripts do not declare reads as 0 or empty.

file.description: A path to write the snapshot to as well, for snapshot_diff to read later.

tools.name: snapshot_diff
tools.description:
Compares two snapshots and says what differs: the same save and inputs run in two engines, or the game at two moments. Pass `a` and `b`, each a snapshot or a file holding one. Creatures are matched by their key (tag|template#k), not by id.

The answer has `same`, `count` and `differences`, each with a JSON pointer `path`, the values `a` and `b`, and `by` for a distance or an amount. Where the game times differ past the tolerance, `skew` is b's minus a's: line the two up before reading the rest. `notCompared` lists fields only one side gave. Needs no game.

a.description: A snapshot as `snapshot` answers it (or another engine writes it, the same schema), or the path of a file holding one.

b.description: A snapshot as `snapshot` answers it (or another engine writes it, the same schema), or the path of a file holding one.

tolerance.description: How far a value may differ and still be the same: position (metres, default 0.01), facing (degrees, 1), health and stamina (points, 0), time (seconds, 0.05: the game time and an effect's time left).

most.description: The most differences to list. Default 200; `count` has them all.

tools.name: stage_cooldown
tools.description: Sets how long is left on a creature's cooldown for one ability; 0 makes the ability ready. `abilities` lists a creature's abilities with their ids. The answer includes the `cooldown` afterwards (`remaining` and `total`). Refuses an ability the creature does not have.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

seconds.description: Seconds left on the cooldown, 0 (ready) to 3600.

total.description: The full length of the cooldown, in seconds. Default: its current length, or `seconds`.

tools.name: stage_cutscene
tools.description: Plays a cutscene the way the game's scripts do. The game's mode changes to cutscene on the next frame (see `health`, or `wait_for` the event eluvian.mode.changed from `cursor`) and stays so until the cutscene ends or is skipped with `dialogue` action=skip_cutscene. Nothing happens if no cutscene has that name.

resource.description: The cutscene's name, such as "bed110cs_tainted_mirror.cut" (.cut is added if missing).

tools.name: stage_effect
tools.description:
Puts a condition on a creature, or removes effects from it, to set up a test.

- `apply`: puts `effect` on the creature for `seconds`, as if from `creator` and `ability` when given.
- `remove`: removes the creature's effects that match `effect`, `ability` and `creator`. With none of them given, removes all its effects.

The answer includes the creature's `effects` afterwards, the `creature` and a `cursor`. The effects are the engine's plain ones, applied the way the game's scripts apply them.

action.description: `apply` to add a condition, `remove` to take effects off.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

effect.description: The condition: stun, knockdown, paralyze, root, sleep, daze, slip, fear, confusion, grabbed, or any EFFECT_TYPE_* number. Required for `apply`.

seconds.description: With `apply`: how long the effect lasts, in seconds, up to 600. Default 6.

creator.description: The creature the effect comes from, by id. Default none.

ability.description: The ability the effect comes from, by id. Default none.

tools.name: stage_equip
tools.description: Creates an item from a template in a creature's inventory and equips it, in the item's own slot or in `slot`. The answer includes the `item` (`item` gives it in full) and whether it was `equipped`; an item the creature cannot use there stays in the backpack. To move items the party already has, use `equip`.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

template.description: The item's template; `resources` with type uti finds them.

slot.description: The slot: main, offhand, ammo, chest, head, boots, gloves, cloak, ring1, ring2, neck or belt. Default: the item's own.

equip.description: Whether to equip it; false leaves it in the backpack. Default true.

tools.name: stage_group
tools.description:
Moves a creature to another group. Groups decide who fights whom: 0 is the player's, 1 the hostile one, 2 friendly, and the game keeps which pairs of groups are hostile.

With `toward`, it first sets whether `group` and the `toward` group are hostile. A spawned creature moved to group 2 fights the hostile creatures near it, which stages a fight without the party.

The answer includes the old group (`was`), the new `group`, and whether it is now `hostileToParty` and `hostileToGroup1`.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

group.description: The group to move it to, 0 to 255.

toward.description: Another group, whose hostility with `group` is set first.

hostile.description: With `toward`: whether the two groups are hostile. Default true.

tools.name: stage_health
tools.description: Sets a creature's current health to `value`. The answer includes the `creature` afterwards. To kill a creature, use `stage_kill`.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

tools.name: stage_kill
tools.description: Kills a creature by dealing it more damage than its health. The death happens a frame or more later: call `wait_for` with the event eluvian.creature.died from the returned `cursor`. If the game is paused, the death waits until it is unpaused (`pause` with paused=false); the answer says `paused`.

id.description: The creature, by id (from `creatures`).

tools.name: stage_reset
tools.description:
Restores things to how they were before a fight, so another fight can run in the same session:
- The party (or the creatures in `ids`) is revived if dead, health and mana or stamina are refilled, and every cooldown is cleared. With `effects`, every effect is removed too.
- Unless `clearDead` is false, creatures that died since the last reset are removed, except the party's. Bodies that were in the area before are left alone.

The answer lists each creature afterwards (`reset`) and what was removed (`removed`).

ids.description: The creatures to reset, by id. Default: the party.

effects.description: Also remove every effect. Default false.

clearDead.description: Remove the creatures that died since the last reset. Default true.

tools.name: stage_spawn
tools.description:
Creates a creature from a template at `point`, in the area of the creature you control.

A template is the game's creature resource, not a kind's name: `creatures` gives each creature's `template`, and `resources` with type utc and a word finds more (for example wolf, ogre_default, hurlock_epic_archer).

The game places the creature at the nearest spot it can stand. `moved` says how far from `point` that was; a point inside a wall may put it in the next room. The creature finishes setting up over the next few frames: wait_for eluvian.creature.ready from `cursor`, then read its health with `creature`. With `group`, it joins that group at once, and the answer says whether it is `hostileToParty`.

point.description: Where to create it: {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

facingDegrees.description: The way it looks, as `creature` reads it: 0 along -y, -90 along +x, 90 along -x, 180 along +y. Default 0.

group.description: The group to put it in, as `stage_group` does.

tools.name: state
tools.description:
Returns the game's current state: the `mode`, whether it is `paused`, the `area`, the `hero`, the creature you control (`controlled`), the party's `leader` (not always the one you control: a follower given control does not lead), the `party` and which members are `selected` in the party bar, the game's message box if one is open (`popup`: its text and buttons), and the event `cursor` to pass as `since` to `events` or `wait_for`.

In combat with no hostile in sight, `combatHold` says why the game stays in combat: it leaves combat only once a living party member stands within 7.5 meters of each fallen one. It lists each fallen member with the nearest living one and how far away it is; walk one there.

tools.name: steer
tools.description:
Holds one of the game's movement keys down for the creature you control, with no key pressed and the window not in front: the creature is steered as by the keyboard, by the engine's own Drive command (`order` with `move` is another thing, a walk to a point). Pass `direction` and `ms`, how long to hold it, or `release: true` to let go of every direction held.

The direction is by the way the camera faces; left and right strafe, they do not turn. The creature runs or walks as the player has it set, and stops when nothing is held. A second direction held while a first still is adds to it (forward and left go diagonally). The game takes movement keys only in explore or combat mode, and not in a conversation or a menu.

The answer says what is `held` and for how many more milliseconds, who is `controlled` (with its position), whether the window is in the `foreground`, and a `cursor`: `wait_for` eluvian.command.started from it shows the Drive command. Each hold ends by itself after its `ms`; read the creature again then to see how far it went.

direction.description: Which movement key to hold, by the camera's facing.

ms.description: How long to hold it, in milliseconds. Default 1000.

release.description: Let go of every direction held, at once.

tools.name: store
tools.description:
Buys or sells an item at the store screen that is open, or closes it. Open a store by talking to a merchant and asking to see the wares.

While a store is open, `gui` reports `fullScreen` Store, and its `store` lists the `stock` with each item's `price`, your `pack` with what each item `sellsFor`, and your `money`, all in copper, as the store itself reckons them.

`action` is one of:
- buy: buys `item` from the stock.
- sell: sells `item` from your pack.
- close: closes the store, as its screen's close does. An item sold can be bought back at what was paid for it only until then.

A buy or sale goes as the screen's own does, and one the screen or the store refuses is an error saying why: not in the stock or pack, a plot item, not enough money, a full backpack, or a store that will not buy it. The answer includes what the `count` cost or fetched (`total`), and the `money` before and after.

action.description: Buy, sell, or close the store.

item.description: With buy or sell: the item, by its id from the `stock` or `pack` that `gui` lists.

count.description: How many of a stack to buy or sell, up to 999. Default 1.

tools.name: surroundings
tools.description: A quick look around, one line per thing: the `creatures`, the placeables that can be used (`usable`: chests, doors, remains, with their state and lock) and the `exits` near a creature, nearest first. Each line is what `creatures`, `placeables` and `exits` return with `brief: true`. Call it on arriving anywhere; use those tools for full detail.

near.description: Look around this creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Only things within this many meters of `near`. Default 30.

tools.name: tactics
tools.description:
Reads and sets a party member's tactics (what they do on their own in a fight), the way the tactics screen does, with no screen open and nobody selected.

`action` is one of:
- look: returns `slots` (how many there are), `ai` (whether the follower's tactics run), `preset` (null when none is chosen), `behaviour`, and `tactics`: each slot in order with `enabled`, `target`, `condition`, `command` and the `ability` or `item` it uses. An unset slot is `empty`.
- choices: returns what the screen offers this party member: the `targets`; with `target`, its `baseConditions`; with `baseCondition` as well, the `conditions`, `actions`, `abilities` and `items`.
- set: sets slot `slot` to `target`, `condition` and `command`, each by number, label or name from what choices offers, with `ability` or `item` for the command and `enabled`. Returns the slot as the game reads it back and whether the change `took`; one the screen would not offer is refused, saying which part.
- clear: empties slot `slot` and returns whether it is `cleared`. Use it to put a party member's tactics back as you found them.
- preset: loads preset `preset` of type `presetType` (0 the AI off, 1 a custom slot, 2 one of the game's, the default) and returns the slots.

id.description: The party member, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

slot.description: For set and clear: the slot, counting from 1. Default 1.

target.description: For choices and set: a target type, by number, label or name.

baseCondition.description: For choices: a base condition, by number, label or name.

condition.description: For set: a condition, by number, label or name.

command.description: For set: the action to take, by number, label or name.

ability.description: For set: the id of the ability the action uses, or the slot a jump goes to.

item.description: For set: the id of the item the action uses.

enabled.description: For set: whether the slot is on. Default true.

preset.description: For preset: the custom slot or the place among the game's presets, from 0. Default 0.

presetType.description: For preset: 0 the AI off, 1 a custom slot, 2 one of the game's. Default 2.

tools.name: travel
tools.description:
Moves a creature, or the party, opening doors on the way. Three kinds of trip:

- Within the area: pass `target` (a creature or object id) or `point`. The creature walks there, opening up to `maxDoors` doors on the way. `upTo` limits the walk to that many meters and reports where it stopped (`cutAt`).
- To another area: pass `exit` (an id from `exits`) or `area` (an area tag; the nearest exit that leads there is used). The creature you control walks to the exit and uses it. The call returns once the new area has loaded.
- Across the world map: pass `to`, a map pin's name, tag or index as `worldmap` lists them, either with the map open or together with the `exit` that opens it.

The answer says whether it `arrived`, the `reason` if not, the `distance` left, the doors it `opened`, and each step. Arrived means within `within` meters, or as close as anyone can stand to a large object such as a door or a chest; use the object from there.

It stops early and says why when a hostile is within `fightNear` meters, a conversation or cutscene starts, the game is paused, or the game shows a message box (answer it with `press`, then travel again). A random encounter on the world map is reported as `encounter`: deal with it, then travel again. The game may autosave on the way. To see what happened during the trip, such as a door that started a fight, call `wait_for` from the returned `cursor`.

id.description: Who walks, by creature id. Default: the creature you control.

target.description: The creature or object to walk to, by id.

point.description: The point to walk to: {x, y, z} or [x, y, z].

exit.description: The exit to use, by its id from `exits`.

area.description: The area to go to, by its tag. The nearest exit that leads there is used.

to.description: A world map pin to travel to: its name (any case), tag or index from `worldmap`.

within.description: How close counts as arrived, in meters. Default 1.5.

upTo.description: With `target` or `point`: walk at most this many meters along the path.

fightNear.description: During combat, keep walking unless a hostile is within this many meters. Default 20; 0 stops for any fight.

maxDoors.description: The most doors to open on the way. Default 4.

budgetMs.description: The longest the call may take, in milliseconds. Default 60000. If it runs out on the way, `note` says so; call travel again to go on.

tools.name: triggers
tools.description:
Lists the area's triggers, nearest first: each one's `id`, `tag`, `name`, `position`, `distance`, whether it is `active`, and `leadsTo` if it takes the party to another area (`exits` lists only those). A trigger is not used but walked into: `travel` or `order` move to its position.

Pass `ints` to read local integer variables on each trigger, as its scripts set them, such as a puzzle's state or a switch's number (returned as `ints`).

near.description: Measure distances from this creature, by id. Default: the creature you control.

radius.description: Only those within this many meters of `near`. Default: the whole area.

tag.description: Only those whose tag contains this, in any case.

ints.description: Names of local integer variables to read on each trigger, up to 32.

tools.name: wait_for
tools.description:
Waits until an event matching `topic` and `match` happens, and returns it. Use it instead of sleeping and reading the log.

The answer has `found`, the `event`, and `next`, the cursor after it. If time runs out, `found` is false and the answer says what is known of why nothing came (for example, the game is `paused`).

topic.description: A topic ("eluvian.command.ended"), a prefix ("mymod.*"), "*", or an array of these. Default: every topic.

match.description: Payload fields the event must have, with equal values; nested objects match as subsets. Creatures are ids like "0x7d9": {"id": "0x7d9"}.

since.description: Look for events from this cursor on. Pass the `cursor` from the answer of the call that set things off, so an event that came before the wait is not missed. Default: from now.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. Default 30000.

tools.name: wait_ready
tools.description:
Waits until the game takes input again, for example after an area exit, a load, the end of a fight or conversation, or a cutscene. It returns when the game is exploring or in combat, the party is dead, the main menu is open, a conversation is at a choice, a message box is open, or a full-screen interface is open (a picker, a map, a store).

The answer includes `ready`, the `mode`, `what` is taking input, and `passed`: the modes, saves and loads gone through on the way. `ready` is false if `timeoutMs` ran out first.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. Default 60000.

intervalMs.description: How often to check the game, in milliseconds. Default 250.

tools.name: wait_until
tools.description:
Waits until a condition on a tool's answer holds. It calls `tool` with `args` every `intervalMs` until the value at `pointer` in the answer meets the expectation (`equals`, `notEquals`, `exists`, `atLeast` or `atMost`), or `timeoutMs` runs out. Use it for a state no event marks: a creature dead, the party's health back, a mode gone. To wait for an event, use `wait_for`.

The answer includes `held`, the last `value`, `tries` and `waitedMs`, and `unmet` or `lastError` when the condition did not hold. A failed call (for example while the game loads) counts as not yet.

tool.description: The tool to call, by name (not `wait_until` or `scenario`).

pointer.description: Where to look in the tool's answer, as a JSON pointer like "/health/current". Default "": the whole answer.

equals.description: Holds when the value equals this.

notEquals.description: Holds when the value is anything but this.

exists.description: Holds when there is (true) or is not (false) a value at `pointer`.

atLeast.description: Holds when the value is a number at least this.

atMost.description: Holds when the value is a number at most this.

intervalMs.description: How often to call the tool, in milliseconds. Default 250.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. Default 30000.

tools.name: warp
tools.description:
Puts the party in an area, at one of its waypoints, by the game's own area transition (DoAreaTransition), with no save there: the area loads and its scripts run as on arriving by its doors, so a cutscene or a fight it starts plays. Use a test save: the area's plot may not be where its scripts expect, and plot sets flags first.

Pass `area`, its tag (state's `area` gives the one the party is in; `resources` with type "are" lists them). `waypoint`, one of the area's, is where the party arrives; without it, the area's own arrival. `waypoints: true` lists the area's waypoints (tag and position) and jumps nowhere. Both are checked against the area's file before anything is sent: the game itself puts the party at (0, 0, 0) for a waypoint the area lacks.

It jumps from explore or combat mode, and answers once the party is in the area, or after `budgetMs`: the `area`, the `party`, the `mode` it arrived in (cutscene, dialog or combat if the area's scripts started one), with a waypoint where the hero stands (`at`) and how far from it (`fromWaypoint`, metres), `arrived`, and a `cursor` for the events of the load.

area.description: The area's tag, as pre440ar_tower_level_4 (the Tower of Ishal's top floor). Without case.

waypoint.description: One of the area's waypoints, by tag. Default: the area's own arrival.

waypoints.description: List the area's waypoints and jump nowhere. Default false.

budgetMs.description: The longest to wait for the area to load, in milliseconds. Default 60000.

tools.name: window
tools.description:
Returns where the game's window is on the desktop, for tests that must use the real mouse: `client`, the top left corner of the game's picture in desktop pixels (`x`, `y`) and its `width` and `height`, and whether the window is `minimised` or the `foreground` window (the one that gets mouse and keyboard input). A copy game_launch started is kept behind the window in front: `keptBehind` counts the game's own calls that would have brought it forward and were made not to.

To click a spot seen in a screenshot, take its position as a fraction of the picture, multiply by the size and add the corner. Works in any mode.

tools.name: worldmap
tools.description:
Returns the world map: whether it is open (`up`), where the party is (`at`, an area tag), and its `pins`. Each pin has an `index`, `name`, `tag`, the `area` it leads to, and a `state`: `active`, `not active`, `greyed`, `unlockable`, `completed` or `destroyed`. Only active pins can be traveled to.

To go to a pin, call `travel` with `to` (the pin's name, tag or index), either with the map open or together with the area's world map exit, which opens it. If the map has never been opened this game, there may be no pins yet.

In a city, the open map may be the city's own: `shown` names the map on screen and `other` the one its toggle button switches to. To switch, call `input` with {"message": "WorldMap.WorldMapSwapMaps"}; `travel` with `to` switches by itself when the pin is on the other map. To close the map, call `input` with {"message": "GUI.HideFullScreenGUI"}, as its Close button does. (WorldMap.WorldMapClosed only reports that the map closed; it does not close it.)
